help.terms.title: Terms
help.terms.body:
Usenet: An old, worldwide network for files. Movies and shows are stored there in many small parts.
Provider: The company that gives you access to Usenet (a subscription). The data comes from there when you play something.
Indexer: A search site for Usenet. It knows where a movie is. You need an account there and an API key. That is a long string that programs use to log in.
Addon: An extension for Nuvio or Stremio. With the addon address the app finds your streams.
AIOStreams: The program on your server. It searches for streams and hands them to your app.
Prowlarr: Manages your indexers. AIOStreams asks the indexers through Prowlarr.
Passkey: A login without a password, e.g. with Face ID or a fingerprint. It is safer than a password.
Backup key: It encrypts your backup. The public part is on the server. Only you have the private part, and only it can open the backup.
help.backup_download.title: Download a backup
help.backup_download.body:
The server makes a backup every Sunday morning. It is encrypted. The two newest are kept.
The files are here:
$ {dir}
Now and then copy the newest backup to your phone or computer, e.g. once a month.
With the Termius app: connect to your server, open SFTP and download the newest file ending in .tar.age.
On a computer in a terminal:
$ scp {user}@{host}:{dir}/*.tar.age .
Restore on a new server: install roadie there. Copy the backup and your backup key to it. Then run:
$ sudo roadie restore BACKUP-FILE --identity KEY-FILE
Afterwards everything works as before, with the same addon addresses.
help.backup_download.no_key: Automatic backups are not set up yet: a backup key is missing. Run sudo roadie and choose 'Change settings'. The wizard then creates one.
help.trouble.title: When something does not work
help.trouble.body:
First choose 'Check status'. It shows which part has a problem.
Streaming problems? Choose 'Check Usenet': it tests every provider and indexer on its own.
No streams? Often an indexer's daily limit is reached. It resets the next day. Or the languages you chose are too narrow.
A service is not running? Choose 'Restart services'. If that does not help, restart the server. It is offline for about two minutes:
$ sudo reboot
Login not working? 'Show login confirmation code' shows the code.
Passkey not working? Wait 5 minutes or choose 'Check status'. Then delete the old passkey in your password app and create it again.
The troubleshooting guide answers the common questions:
$ https://github.com/usenetroadie/roadie/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md
Still stuck? Ask at roadie – questions are welcome, also small ones:
$ https://github.com/usenetroadie/roadie/issues/new/choose
Please do not ask in the communities of AIOStreams, Prowlarr, Authelia or Traefik first. Your server is set up the roadie way: its own login in front, its own firewall rules, fixed versions, settings that roadie writes. The people there do not know this setup, and they run their projects in their free time. A roadie question costs them time and rarely helps you. Here it can be answered – and if the cause really lies in one of those programs, roadie reports it there properly, with everything they need to fix it.
Put this in your question:
- what you did, what you expected and what happened instead
- the version: roadie --version
- the problem report:
$ sudo roadie diagnose
The report leaves out passwords, keys, IP addresses and your domain. Read it once before you post it anyway – you know your server best.
Never post your addon address, passwords, API keys or your backup key.
A security problem (someone could get in, or see something they should not)? Report it privately, not as a public issue:
$ https://github.com/usenetroadie/roadie/security/advisories/new
help.next_steps.title: Next steps
help.next_steps.body:
1. Install Nuvio (phone, tablet, TV) or Stremio. Add your addon address there under Addons. You can find it under 'Show my access details'.
2. Open the settings page and log in. On the first login, set up a passkey or a code app.
3. If not done yet: install the ntfy app and subscribe to your topic. Then your server reports problems to your phone.
help.next_steps.backup: 4. Your first backup is made on Sunday around 04:07 – or right now with: sudo roadie → 'Create a backup now'. Then download it. How: see Help → Download a backup.
help.do_it_yourself.title: Adjust it yourself
help.do_it_yourself.body:
AIOStreams: open the settings page. Load your configuration with UUID and config password (under 'Show my access details'). Change what you like and save. It takes effect right away.
The wizard only sets languages, quality (with HDR), Usenet streaming, TMDB, sorting and its own addons. With 'Change settings' and with updates it only sets these parts again. Everything else stays, including your own addons.
Stream limit (5 per resolution, 20 in total): under Filters → Result Limits. The wizard sets it only the first time, your changes stay.
Prowlarr: open the indexer management (same login). Under Indexers you add indexers and test them. Then choose 'Restart services' in sudo roadie. Only then does AIOStreams know the new indexers. The wizard deletes nothing in Prowlarr.

help.more_catalogs.title: More catalogs
help.more_catalogs.body:
Catalogs are the rows on the start page of your app. The wizard sets up a few classics: trending, big streaming services, movie collections. Under Addons → Catalogs you show or hide rows. You get more with other catalog addons:
AIOMetadata: with a TMDB key the wizard already set up your own (address under 'Show my access details'). There you add or remove catalogs.
Watchly, MyTrakt, Simkl: rows from your own history, e.g. suggestions. You need an account with that service.
How to add an addon: set it up on its website and copy its addon address (ends with manifest.json). On the AIOStreams settings page, load your configuration. On the Addons page, click the line about an addon that is not in the Marketplace, paste the address and save. All this stays, the wizard does not change it.
open.catalogs: The start page of your app stays empty: the catalog addons did not answer. Usually it works later by itself. Otherwise run: sudo roadie setup and choose 'Continue / check everything again'.

q.tmdb.step3: 3. Copy the 'API Read Access Token' and paste it here right away.

cli.cmd.explain: help pages, and what is installed, how it fits together and how to look after it yourself
explain.overview.title: How it all fits together
explain.overview.body:
Your server runs a few programs, each in its own container. A container is a sealed box with one program and everything it needs. Docker starts the boxes and connects them in a private network.
What happens when you press play:
1. Your app (Nuvio, Stremio) asks https://aiostreams.{domain} for streams.
2. Traefik receives the request. It is the only program the internet can reach, and it holds the HTTPS certificate.
3. Traefik hands the request to AIOStreams. AIOStreams asks Prowlarr, and Prowlarr asks your indexers where the movie is.
4. AIOStreams fetches the parts from your Usenet provider and streams them straight to your app. Nothing is kept for good.
Settings pages are guarded by Authelia: before Traefik lets you in, Authelia checks your login.
Around all this, the server protects itself (firewall, fail2ban, security updates) and roadie looks after it (watcher, push messages, backups).
The other topics explain each part, with the commands to look at it yourself.
How would you build all this by hand? Every step, every file and the reason behind it is in the guide:
$ https://github.com/usenetroadie/roadie/blob/main/docs/manual-setup.md
explain.services.title: The services
explain.services.body:
Each box below is one container on this server: what it does, where its page is, where its files are, and how to read its log. A log is the diary of a program: when something goes wrong, the reason is almost always in there.
All files are in {stack}.
explain.svc.unknown: Not set up by roadie: you added it to compose.yaml yourself.
explain.svc.traefik.name: Traefik – the front door
explain.svc.traefik.what: Receives every request from the internet on ports 80 and 443 and sends it on by its address: aiostreams.… to AIOStreams, auth.… to Authelia and so on. It gets the HTTPS certificate from Let's Encrypt and renews it by itself.
explain.svc.traefik.files: Settings: config/traefik/traefik.yml (how Traefik starts) and config/traefik/routes.yml (which address goes where; Traefik notices changes at once). Data: data/traefik/acme.json (the certificate) and data/traefik/access.log (one line per request – fail2ban reads it to spot attackers).
explain.svc.authelia.name: Authelia – the login
explain.svc.authelia.what: Checks who you are before Traefik opens a settings page: password plus passkey or code app. Your player apps do not need it: the addon paths are open for them, and only for reading.
explain.svc.authelia.files: Settings: config/authelia/configuration.yml (which address needs which login) and config/authelia/users.yml (your user and a hash of your password, never the password itself). Data: data/authelia/db.sqlite3 (passkeys, code app). One-time codes land in data/authelia/notification.txt – 'sudo roadie code' shows them.
explain.svc.aiostreams.name: AIOStreams – the heart
explain.svc.aiostreams.what: The addon your apps talk to. It searches through Prowlarr, sorts and filters the results by your settings and streams from your Usenet provider. Change its settings on its web page: load your configuration with UUID and config password ('sudo roadie access').
explain.svc.aiostreams.files: Settings for the whole server: env/aiostreams.env (Usenet providers, passwords – secret). Your configurations: data/aiostreams/db.sqlite. data/aiostreams/cache holds parts of recently played files; it may be deleted, it fills up again.
explain.svc.prowlarr.name: Prowlarr – the indexer manager
explain.svc.prowlarr.what: Holds your indexer accounts and asks all of them at once. Add, test or remove indexers on its web page. AIOStreams reads the indexer list only when it starts: after a change run 'sudo roadie restart'.
explain.svc.prowlarr.files: Settings: env/prowlarr.env (its API key). Data: data/prowlarr (indexers, history, its own logs in data/prowlarr/logs).
explain.svc.aiometadata.name: AIOMetadata – catalogs and details
explain.svc.aiometadata.what: Fills the start page of your app with rows (trending, popular, …) and shows the details of movies and shows, from TMDB and in your language. AIOStreams reaches it inside the server; on its web page (…/configure) you add, hide or reorder rows.
explain.svc.aiometadata.files: Settings: env/aiometadata.env (your TMDB key – secret). Data: data/aiometadata (your catalog configuration).
explain.svc.aiometadata-redis.name: Redis – memory for AIOMetadata
explain.svc.aiometadata-redis.what: A fast store where AIOMetadata keeps what it already fetched from TMDB, so pages load quickly. Not reachable from outside; you never need to touch it.
explain.svc.aiometadata-redis.files: Data: data/aiometadata-redis (only a cache – losing it costs nothing but a slower first start).
explain.svc.status.name: Status page
explain.svc.status.what: A tiny web server that shows one page: is everything running, open problems, last backup, updates. The watcher writes the page every 5 minutes.
explain.svc.status.files: Data: data/status/index.html (plain HTML, read only for the web server).
explain.network.title: Doors and locks: ports and firewall
explain.network.body:
A port is a numbered door of your server. Only these are open to the internet:
- {ssh_ports}: SSH, your terminal login. Only with your key and only for the user {user}.
- 80: HTTP. Only sends visitors on to 443, and lets Let's Encrypt check your address for the certificate.
- 443: HTTPS. All web traffic: your apps and the settings pages. Traefik decides by the address where a request goes.
Everything else listens only inside Docker's private network: AIOStreams on 3000, Prowlarr on 9696 and so on. From outside you reach them only through Traefik – and through the login.
The firewall (UFW) keeps every other door shut:
$ sudo ufw status verbose
Good to know: Docker opens its ports past UFW. That is why only Traefik opens any.
Which program listens on which port:
$ sudo ss -tlnp
fail2ban watches the logins and blocks addresses that try too often:
- sshd: 3 failed SSH logins within 10 minutes: blocked for 1 hour, longer each time (up to 1 week)
- sshd-invalid: 3 tries with a user name that does not exist: blocked for 1 hour (up to 4 weeks)
- traefik-scanner: bots that probe for weak spots (/.env, wp-login, .php …): blocked for 1 day (up to 4 weeks)
- recidive: blocked 3 times in one day: blocked for 1 week on every port
Who is blocked right now, and how to unblock an address:
$ sudo fail2ban-client status sshd
$ sudo fail2ban-client set sshd unbanip 203.0.113.10
explain.files.title: Where everything is
explain.files.body:
{stack} – everything the services need:
- compose.yaml: the list of containers – program, version, memory limit, folders. Docker builds the containers from it.
- config/: settings files of Traefik and Authelia
- env/: settings and passwords of each service (only root may read them)
- secrets/: keys for Authelia (only root)
- data/: what the services store – databases, certificates, logs, cache. This is what a backup is for.
/etc/roadie – roadie's own files: your answers (state.json), every generated password (secrets.json, only root) and your addon addresses.
/var/lib/roadie – what the watcher remembers between its runs.
{backup_dir} – your encrypted backups.
System files roadie writes:
- /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-roadie.conf: rules for SSH
- /etc/fail2ban/jail.d/roadie.conf: rules for fail2ban
- /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/99zz-roadie: automatic updates
- /etc/systemd/system/roadie-*: the scheduled jobs
Important: a file that starts with 'Generated by roadie' is written again by every 'sudo roadie setup' and every update. Change those through roadie ('Change settings'). What you change on the web pages (AIOStreams, Prowlarr, AIOMetadata) is kept in data/ and stays.
Look around (only reading, nothing changes):
$ sudo ls -la {stack} {stack}/data
$ sudo cat {stack}/compose.yaml
explain.jobs.title: What runs by itself
explain.jobs.body:
- Every 5 minutes: the watcher checks the services, your address from outside, the certificate, disk and memory. It sends a push message when something is wrong, and again when it is fixed.
- Sunday around 04:07: an encrypted backup. The apps stop for about a minute, Traefik keeps running.
- Sunday 10:13: the weekly report as a push message.{duckdns}
- Every day: security updates for the system. If one needs a restart, the server restarts at {reboot}.
- Traefik renews the HTTPS certificate by itself, about 30 days before it runs out.
The schedule and when each job ran last:
$ systemctl list-timers 'roadie-*'
What a job did (its log):
$ journalctl -u roadie-watch -n 30
$ journalctl -u roadie-backup -n 30
Pause the watcher while you try something, then switch it on again:
$ sudo systemctl stop roadie-watch.timer
$ sudo systemctl start roadie-watch.timer
explain.jobs.duckdns: - Every 5 minutes: your DuckDNS address is pointed at the server's current IP address (roadie-duckdns).
explain.docker.title: Working with the containers yourself
explain.docker.body:
Docker commands work from the stack folder:
$ cd {stack}
Which containers run, and are they healthy:
$ sudo docker compose ps
The last lines of a log (any service name instead of aiostreams):
$ sudo docker compose logs --tail 50 aiostreams
Follow a log live (end with Ctrl+C):
$ sudo docker compose logs -f aiostreams
Restart one service:
$ sudo docker compose restart prowlarr
Memory and CPU of each container:
$ sudo docker stats --no-stream
After you changed compose.yaml or a file in env/ yourself, let Docker build the changed containers new so they read it:
$ sudo docker compose up -d
Good to know:
- 'restart' starts the same container again. 'up -d' builds it new from compose.yaml when something changed. Your data in data/ stays either way.
- roadie installs fixed, tested versions. Leave the versions in compose.yaml to 'sudo roadie update' – it would replace your own.
- Never delete the data/ folder: your settings, logins and configurations are in there.
Without roadie – the same jobs by hand:
- Backup: stop the apps, copy the whole stack folder (above all data/, env/, config/, secrets/ and compose.yaml) somewhere safe (it contains your passwords – keep it private), start them again:
$ sudo docker compose stop && sudo tar -czf ~/stack-backup.tar.gz -C {stack} . && sudo docker compose start
- Update a service: put the new version (the 'tag') behind its image in compose.yaml, read its release notes first, then:
$ sudo docker compose pull && sudo docker compose up -d
- Watching: 'sudo docker compose ps' shows unhealthy containers; the logs say why.
explain.security.title: How your server is protected
explain.security.body:
Server login: only with your SSH key and only as {user}. Passwords and the root user are switched off for SSH once your key login worked. {user} may run commands as administrator with sudo.
Settings pages: Authelia asks for your password plus a passkey or a code from your app. The password is stored only as a hash – a fingerprint that cannot be turned back into the password.
Apps: your addon address contains a long secret code. Whoever has the address can stream, so only share it with people you trust. To lock someone out, remove the person under 'Manage people'.
Secrets: all generated passwords are in /etc/roadie/secrets.json and the env/ files, readable only by root. 'sudo roadie access' shows the ones you need.
Backups: encrypted with age. Only your private backup key can open them, and it is not on the server.
Updates: roadie installs only releases with a valid signature. The system installs security updates every day.
Check it yourself:
$ sudo sshd -T | grep -E '^(passwordauthentication|permitrootlogin|allowusers)'
$ sudo ufw status
$ sudo fail2ban-client status
explain.why: Why it is set up like this:
explain.overview.why:
Why so many parts and not one big program? Each part is the best known tool for one job, used by many thousands of servers, and updated by its own team. roadie does not rebuild any of them – it puts them together, sets them up safely and keeps an eye on them. That is also why you can learn each of them on its own, and why their own manuals apply to your server.
Why containers? Each program brings exactly the versions of everything it needs, so they never get in each other's way, and an update replaces the box without leaving rubbish on the system. If something breaks, you restart one box, not the server.
explain.svc.traefik.why: Without it, every program would need its own open port and its own certificate. With one front door there is a single place for HTTPS, a single place where the login is checked and a single log of who knocked. Traefik reads its routes from a file instead of from Docker, so it needs no access to Docker itself – a break-in into Traefik does not give control over the server.
explain.svc.authelia.why: AIOStreams and Prowlarr have their own simple logins or none at all, and their settings pages hold your provider password and API keys. Authelia puts one strong login in front of all of them, with a second factor, so a guessed or leaked password alone is not enough. It keeps its data in one small file (SQLite), because a few users need no database server.
explain.svc.aiostreams.why: Players like Nuvio and Stremio ask addons for streams. AIOStreams is one addon that asks many sources, removes duplicates, sorts by your rules and – since version 2 – streams Usenet itself, without a download program. That is why one address in your app is enough.
explain.svc.prowlarr.why: Every indexer has its own address, key and limits. Prowlarr keeps them in one place, watches the daily limits and pauses an indexer that fails, so AIOStreams only needs one connection. You change indexers there without touching AIOStreams.
explain.svc.aiometadata.why: Without it the start page uses a public catalog server that many people share. Your own AIOMetadata uses your TMDB key, shows titles in your language and lets you decide which rows appear.
explain.svc.aiometadata-redis.why: AIOMetadata needs a fast memory to keep TMDB answers; otherwise every page would ask TMDB again and the start page would be slow.
explain.svc.status.why: Not everyone wants to open a terminal to see whether all is well. The page is plain HTML without any program code, written by the watcher – so it shows something even when other services are down.
explain.network.why:
Every open door is a door someone can try. Bots try thousands of servers every day – that is normal and not aimed at you. So only three doors are open, and everything behind them needs a login.
SSH with a key instead of a password: a key cannot be guessed, a password can. roadie switches passwords off only after it saw your key working, so you cannot lock yourself out.
fail2ban: even with a key, endless tries fill the logs and cost resources. Blocking an address after a few tries stops this. The time grows with every block, so persistent bots stay away for longer.
explain.files.why:
Generated files are written again on purpose: so an update can bring better settings, and a setting that was changed by accident is fixed on the next run. Your own changes belong on the web pages – they are kept in data/ and roadie never touches them.
Secrets are kept apart from settings and readable only by root, so a mistake in a settings file or a screenshot of it does not reveal a password.
All data of the services is in one folder (data/). That keeps a backup small and a move to a new server simple: copy one folder, start again.
explain.jobs.why:
A server that nobody watches breaks quietly. The watcher tells you before you notice it on the TV – and only once, with a reminder after 12 hours, so the messages stay worth reading.
Backups run weekly and the two newest are kept: enough to go back a week, small enough not to fill the disk. They are only useful if you download one now and then.
Security updates install by themselves because most break-ins use holes that were already fixed. A restart happens only when an update needs one, and at night.
explain.docker.why:
roadie pins fixed versions on purpose. A new version of AIOStreams or Authelia can change settings or behaviour; roadie only switches after the whole setup was tested with it. That is why 'latest' is never used.
You can always look and read logs – nothing breaks from that. Changing files by hand is fine too, but remember which ones roadie writes again (topic 'Where everything is').
explain.security.why: No single protection is perfect, so there are several layers: if one fails, the next one still holds. A leaked Authelia password still needs your second factor; an SSH password cannot even be tried; an open port that should not be there is closed by the firewall; a known hole is closed by the daily updates. And if everything goes wrong, the encrypted backup brings the server back.
